RE: LULAC Comments on Proposed Rule CMS-0062-P (RIN 0938-AV44), Medicare 
and Medicaid Programs; Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act; Interoperability 
Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs 
 
Dear Administrator Oz: 
 
On behalf of the League of United Latin American Citizens (LULAC), the nation's oldest 
and largest Latino civil rights organization, representing more than 570,000 members and 
more than 435 councils across the United States, we respectfully submit these comments 
regarding the proposed rule, CMS-0062-P (RIN 0938-AV44), Medicare and Medicaid 
Programs; Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act; Interoperability Standards and 
Prior Authorization for Drugs. 
 
LULAC supports CMS's effort to modernize the prior authorization process through 
electronic interoperability, standardized data exchange, and improved reporting 
requirements. According to the April 14, 2026 proposed rule, Medicare and Medicaid 
Programs; Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act; Interoperability Standards and 
Prior Authorization for Drugs, CMS seeks to improve the electronic exchange of health 
information, standardize prior authorization processes, and increase transparency across 
Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, and Qualified Health Plans. 
 
These are worthy goals. Administrative complexity should not stand between patients 
and medically necessary care. Electronic interoperability can reduce paperwork, improve 
communication between providers and health plans, and shorten unnecessary delays. 
 
Yet this proposal leaves unanswered the most important question before the agency.  Will 
patients be more likely to receive the care their physicians prescribe?  The rule makes 
prior authorization more transparent. It does not necessarily make it more accountable.  
Throughout the proposal, CMS requires plans to report denial rates, appeal outcomes, 
utilization management metrics, and standardized denial codes. Those requirements will  
 
League of United Latin American Citizens 
 
 
1150 18th Street, NW, Suite 650 â€¢ Washington, DC 20036 â€¢ (202) 833-6130 â€¢ FAX (202) 833-6135 â€¢ www.LULAC.org 
produce more information about how prior authorization operates. They will make the system more visible 
to regulators, providers, and patients. 
 
Visibility, however, is not reform. Transparency is valuable only if it produces accountability. Data that 
simply document failure without requiring corrective action risk normalizing the very practices they are 
intended to expose. A system that measures inequity but does not correct it has merely become more 
sophisticated at observing injustice. 
 
Technology can make prior authorization faster.  Transparency can make it more visible.  Only accountability 
can make it fair.  For that reason, LULAC respectfully urges CMS to strengthen the final rule by ensuring 
that every transparency provision is paired with meaningful enforcement and measurable accountability. 
 
Concern 1: Interoperability Must Improve Care, Not Simply Accelerate Denials 
 
LULAC supports CMS's adoption of Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR)-based application 
programming interfaces, standardized electronic prior authorization workflows, and standardized denial 
reason codes. These innovations represent meaningful progress toward reducing administrative complexity 
and modernizing healthcare delivery. 
 
However, the proposal largely focuses on improving the speed and efficiency of prior authorization 
transactions rather than the quality of the decisions being made. 
 
According to the 2026 Kaiser Family Foundation report, Medicare Advantage Insurers Made Nearly 53 
Million Prior Authorization Determinations in 2024, Medicare Advantage plans processed nearly 53 million 
prior authorization requests and denied approximately 4.1 million of them. Only 11.5 percent of those denials 
were appealed, yet more than 80 percent of appealed denials were ultimately overturned. 
 
Those numbers tell a story. They suggest not a system that occasionally makes mistakes but one in which 
many patients never receive the care they need because they cannot challenge an initial denial. 
 
According to the American Medical Association's 2025 report, Fixing Prior Auth: Nearly 40 Prior 
Authorizations a Week Is Way Too Many, 94 percent of physicians report that prior authorization harms 
clinical outcomes, while nearly one-third have witnessed a serious adverse event attributable to prior 
authorization delays. 
 
The proposed rule makes denials arrive more quickly and explains them more clearly. It does not substantially 
reduce their occurrence. A denial delivered electronically in twenty-four hours instead of seven days remains 
a denial. The measure of interoperability should not be administrative efficiency alone. It should be whether 
patients receive medically necessary care more quickly and whether inappropriate denials become less 
common. Technology should improve care, not simply accelerate the mechanisms that delay it. 
 
Concern 2: Transparency Without Accountability Is Not Reform 
 
 
League of United Latin American Citizens 
 
 
1150 18th Street, NW, Suite 650 â€¢ Washington, DC 20036 â€¢ (202) 833-6130 â€¢ FAX (202) 833-6135 â€¢ www.LULAC.org 
LULAC supports the transparency requirements contained in this proposed rule. Public reporting of approval 
rates, denial rates, appeal volumes, and appeal outcomes will give policymakers, providers, and patients a 
clearer picture of how prior authorization functions across the healthcare system. 
 
But transparency is not the same as accountability. 
 
According to the 2026 proposed rule, Medicare and Medicaid Programs; Patient Protection and Affordable 
Care Act; Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs, CMS proposes new reporting 
requirements for prior authorization metrics while stopping short of establishing enforcement mechanisms 
tied to excessive denial rates, high appeal overturn rates, or persistent disparities in patient outcomes. 
 
This distinction matters. 
 
The federal government already knows that prior authorization delays care. It already knows that physicians 
spend countless hours navigating utilization management requirements. It already knows that many denials 
are overturned when appealed. Publishing more data about these problems will not solve them unless those 
data compel action. 
 
Transparency, by itself, asks institutions to confess.  Accountability requires them to change.  A health plan 
with denial rates far above national averages should not simply file another report the following year. A plan 
whose denials are routinely overturned should not merely explain its numbers in a compliance document. If 
the data reveal a pattern of inappropriate decision-making, the agency should intervene. 
 
Otherwise, transparency becomes little more than recordkeeping. 
 
The purpose of collecting information is not to create larger databases. It is to improve public policy. Data 
should lead to oversight. Oversight should lead to corrective action. Corrective action should lead to better 
care for patients. 
 
Without that chain of responsibility, reporting requirements become administrative exercises disconnected 
from the lives they are intended to protect. 
 
CMS has an opportunity to build a prior authorization system that is not only more transparent but more 
accountable. That means establishing objective thresholds that trigger regulatory review when denial rates 
substantially exceed national norms, when appeal overturn rates indicate systemic failures in clinical 
judgment, or when reporting reveals persistent disparities affecting Latino beneficiaries, patients with limited 
English proficiency, or other protected populations. 
 
Transparency should illuminate problems. 
 
Accountability should solve them. 
 
 
League of United Latin American Citizens 
 
 
1150 18th Street, NW, Suite 650 â€¢ Washington, DC 20036 â€¢ (202) 833-6130 â€¢ FAX (202) 833-6135 â€¢ www.LULAC.org 
The final rule should ensure that reporting is not the end of the regulatory process but the beginning of 
meaningful oversight. 
 
Concern 3: Latino Communities Bear a Disproportionate Burden 
 
The failures of the current prior authorization system do not fall evenly across the American population. 
They fall most heavily on communities that already experience barriers to healthcare. 
 
According to the 2025 analysis, Checking the Facts on Medicaid Use by Latinos, nearly one-third of the 
Latino population is enrolled in Medicaid. 
 
According to the Pew Research Center's 2025 report, What the Data Says About Medicaid, Hispanic 
Americans comprise approximately 31 percent of Medicaid enrollees despite representing a much smaller 
share of the national population. 
 
According to the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services' 2023 report, Projected Impacts for Latino 
Medicare Enrollees, Latino Medicare beneficiaries experience significantly higher rates of diabetes, 
hypertension, disability, and difficulty affording prescription medications than White beneficiaries. 
 
These statistics describe a population with greater medical need and fewer resources to absorb delays in care.  
According to the 2024 study, Racial and Ethnic Disparities in Prior Authorizations for Patients with Cancer, 
Hispanic patients experience higher prior authorization denial rates than other patient populations. 
 
Yet the proposed rule contains no mechanism for determining whether these disparities improve after 
implementation. Transparency that cannot identify inequity is incomplete. Transparency that identifies 
inequity but requires no corrective action is insufficient. CMS should require demographic reporting and 
establish enforcement mechanisms that respond when disparities persist. Health equity requires 
accountability. 
 
Concern 4: Pharmacy Benefit Manager Transparency Must Produce Patient Benefit 
 
The proposal increases transparency surrounding prescription drug prior authorization and formulary 
management. According to the 2026 proposed rule, Medicare and Medicaid Programs; Patient Protection 
and Affordable Care Act; Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs, plans will provide 
greater transparency regarding electronic prescription drug prior authorization and standardized denial 
reporting. 
 
This information will be valuable. But information alone will not reduce patient costs or improve access to 
medication. Patients continue to encounter rebate-driven formularies, step therapy requirements, and 
utilization management policies that delay access to physician-prescribed treatment. 
 
 
League of United Latin American Citizens 
 
 
1150 18th Street, NW, Suite 650 â€¢ Washington, DC 20036 â€¢ (202) 833-6130 â€¢ FAX (202) 833-6135 â€¢ www.LULAC.org 
Transparency that leaves these incentives untouched merely documents unaffordability rather than correcting 
it. The purpose of transparency should be to expose practices that require reform. Without reform, 
transparency serves administrators more than patients. 
 
Concern 5: Language Access Is a Legal Obligation, Not a Technical Afterthought 
 
Electronic interoperability cannot achieve its purpose if patients cannot understand the information they 
receive. According to the 2025 study, MedCOD: Enhancing English-to-Spanish Medical Translation of Large 
Language Models Using Enriched Chain-of-Dictionary Framework, approximately one-third of Hispanic 
adults with limited English proficiency report difficulty understanding physician instructions and completing 
medical forms. 
 
According to the Kaiser Family Foundation's 2023 report, Overview of Health Coverage and Care for 
Individuals with Limited English Proficiency, individuals with limited English proficiency face significantly 
greater barriers to healthcare access than English-proficient populations. Meaningful interoperability requires 
meaningful communication. 
 
CMS should require that denial notices, appeal instructions, and all patient-facing electronic communications 
be available in the patient's preferred language. Digital modernization that excludes millions of patients 
because of language barriers is not modernization at all. 
 
Concern 6: Reporting Without Enforcement Leaves Patients Unprotected 
 
The greatest weakness of this proposal is not its reporting framework. It is the absence of consequences when 
reporting reveals failure. According to the 2026 Kaiser Family Foundation report, Medicare Advantage 
Insurers Made Nearly 53 Million Prior Authorization Determinations in 2024, some Medicare Advantage 
organizations reported denial rates substantially above industry averages while others experienced appeal 
overturn rates exceeding 90 percent. 
 
Those findings should not simply appear in annual reports. They should trigger investigation. They should 
trigger corrective action. They should trigger enforcement. The purpose of collecting data is not to improve 
spreadsheets. It is to improve people's lives. 
 
Without accountability, transparency becomes observation rather than reform. The success of this rule should 
not be measured by how quickly information moves between computers. It should be measured by whether 
fewer patients are denied medically necessary care. Technology can make prior authorization faster. 
Transparency can make it more visible. Only accountability can make it fair. 
 
Recommendations 
 
LULAC respectfully urges CMS to: 
1. Establish enforceable accountability standards tied to denial rates and appeal overturn rates. 
 
League of United Latin American Citizens 
 
 
1150 18th Street, NW, Suite 650 â€¢ Washington, DC 20036 â€¢ (202) 833-6130 â€¢ FAX (202) 833-6135 â€¢ www.LULAC.org 
2. Require automatic regulatory review when denial rates or appeal overturn rates exceed evidence-
based thresholds. 
3. Extend enforcement authority to plans demonstrating persistent patterns of inappropriate denials. 
4. Require demographic reporting and corrective action when disparities are identified. 
5. Mandate multilingual access for all patient-facing electronic communications. 
6. Pair every transparency provision with a corresponding accountability mechanism. 
7. Measure success by improved patient outcomes and reduced inappropriate denials rather than 
administrative efficiency alone. 
 
Conclusion 
 
This proposal has the potential to modernize prior authorization. Whether it reforms prior authorization 
remains an open question. The American people do not need a system that produces better reports about 
delayed care. They need a system that produces less delayed care. Transparency is essential. But transparency 
is not the destination. Accountability is. 
 
The final rule should ensure that information leads to oversight, oversight leads to enforcement, and 
enforcement leads to better patient outcomes. Otherwise, CMS will have created a more efficient system for 
documenting injustice while leaving the injustice itself intact. Technology can make prior authorization faster. 
Transparency can make it more visible. Only accountability can make it fair. 
 
Respectfully submitted, 
 
 
 
Roman Palomares 
LULAC National President and Board Chairman

# Comment Analysis Template: CMS-2026-1255-0001

## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** League of United Latin American Citizens (LULAC); signed by Roman Palomares, National President and Board Chairman
- **Stakeholder type:** Advocacy Group
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** Describes itself as the nation's oldest and largest Latino civil rights organization, representing more than 570,000 members and more than 435 councils across the United States. Lead reviewers listed as Miguel Diaz Gutierrez, Christian Acosta Zuniga, and Steven Gaytan.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

LULAC supports CMS's interoperability and transparency goals but argues the proposed rule must pair reporting with enforceable accountability. It urges CMS to establish denial-rate and appeal-overturn thresholds, require demographic disparity reporting and corrective action, mandate multilingual patient-facing communications, and measure success by reduced inappropriate denials and improved patient outcomes rather than transaction speed alone.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; FHIR-IG-REQUIRED; PA-DENIAL-REASONS; PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS; API-USAGE-METRICS; GENERAL (prior authorization accountability, demographic reporting, language access, PBM/formulary transparency)
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** CMS-0062-P; RIN 0938-AV44; April 14, 2026 proposed rule; no CFR sections cited directly.
- **Standards referenced:** FHIR-based application programming interfaces; standardized electronic prior authorization workflows; standardized denial reason codes. No NCPDP standards are named, though prescription drug prior authorization and formulary management are discussed.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: Interoperability must improve care, not just speed denials**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; FHIR-IG-REQUIRED
- **Position:** Support / Modify
- **Rationale:** LULAC supports FHIR-based APIs, electronic PA workflows, and standardized denial codes, but argues the proposal focuses too much on transaction efficiency and not enough on whether patients receive medically necessary care.
- **Specific request:** Evaluate success by reduced inappropriate denials, improved patient outcomes, and faster access to physician-prescribed care, not administrative speed alone.

**Topic 2: Transparency must trigger accountability**
- **Provision ID:** API-USAGE-METRICS; PA-DENIAL-REASONS; GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** LULAC supports reporting denial rates, appeal outcomes, utilization management metrics, and denial codes but argues that data collection without consequences risks normalizing harmful practices.
- **Specific request:** Pair every transparency provision with enforcement and measurable accountability, including objective thresholds for denial and appeal-overturn rates.

**Topic 3: Enforcement for high denial and overturn rates**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** LULAC cites high Medicare Advantage prior authorization volume, low appeal rates, and high reversal rates as evidence that many patients may not receive needed care because they cannot challenge initial denials.
- **Specific request:** Require automatic regulatory review, corrective action, and enforcement when denial rates or appeal-overturn rates exceed evidence-based thresholds or national norms.

**Topic 4: Health equity and Latino beneficiary impacts**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** LULAC argues Latino communities disproportionately rely on Medicaid and Medicare, experience greater chronic disease and affordability barriers, and may face higher PA denial rates, making PA reform a civil rights and equity issue.
- **Specific request:** Require demographic reporting and corrective action when disparities persist for Latino beneficiaries, patients with limited English proficiency, or other protected populations.

**Topic 5: PBM and formulary transparency**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** LULAC says prescription drug PA and formulary transparency are valuable but insufficient if rebate-driven formularies, step therapy, and utilization management policies continue to delay physician-prescribed treatment.
- **Specific request:** Use transparency to expose and reform practices that increase costs or delay medication access, rather than merely documenting them.

**Topic 6: Language access for patient-facing communications**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DENIAL-REASONS; GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** LULAC argues electronic interoperability fails if patients cannot understand denial notices, appeal instructions, or other patient-facing electronic communications.
- **Specific request:** Require all patient-facing electronic communications, including denial notices and appeal instructions, to be available in the patient's preferred language.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

**Solicitation Responses:**
- **S1:** LULAC supports FHIR-based APIs and standardized electronic PA workflows, but asks CMS to ensure these standards improve care rather than merely accelerate denials.
- **S16:** LULAC supports standardized denial explanations and argues denial data should be tied to accountability when patterns indicate inappropriate decision-making.
- **S17:** LULAC supports standardized denial reason codes as part of transparency, while emphasizing that codes must lead to oversight and corrective action.
- **S20:** LULAC references faster denial delivery, including a 24-hour example, to argue that speed alone is inadequate if inappropriate denials persist.
- **S22:** LULAC raises prescription drug PA and formulary-management concerns, focusing on whether transparency produces patient benefit rather than only administrative information.
- **S29:** LULAC supports reporting approval rates, denial rates, appeal volumes, appeal outcomes, utilization management metrics, and related data, but wants metrics tied to enforcement thresholds.
- **S30:** LULAC requests demographic reporting to identify disparities affecting Latino beneficiaries, patients with limited English proficiency, and other protected populations.
- **S34:** LULAC implies that repeated annual reporting is inadequate without action when high denial or overturn rates persist.
- **S35:** LULAC supports public reporting but argues publication must lead to oversight, corrective action, and enforcement.
- **S66-S82:** LULAC responds to broader prior authorization and health equity concerns by requesting accountability standards, demographic disparity reporting, PBM/formulary transparency that benefits patients, and multilingual patient communications.

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Establish enforceable accountability standards tied to denial rates and appeal overturn rates.
2. Require automatic regulatory review when denial rates or appeal overturn rates exceed evidence-based thresholds.
3. Extend enforcement authority to plans with persistent inappropriate denial patterns.
4. Require demographic reporting and corrective action when disparities are identified.
5. Mandate multilingual access for all patient-facing electronic communications, including denial notices and appeal instructions.
6. Pair every transparency provision with a corresponding accountability mechanism.
7. Measure success by improved patient outcomes and reduced inappropriate denials rather than administrative efficiency alone.
8. Ensure prescription drug and PBM/formulary transparency produces patient access and affordability benefits.

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** Transparency without accountability; faster electronic denials that do not reduce inappropriate denials; disproportionate effects on Latino communities; lack of demographic reporting; insufficient language access; PBM and utilization management incentives that continue to delay care.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** Delayed medically necessary care, unappealed denials, serious adverse events from PA delays, higher burdens on Latino beneficiaries and limited-English-proficient patients, and documentation of inequity without correction.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** No technical implementation barriers are emphasized; LULAC focuses on regulatory design, enforcement thresholds, demographic data collection, language access, and corrective action.

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** KFF 2026 report: nearly 53 million Medicare Advantage PA determinations in 2024, approximately 4.1 million denials, 11.5 percent appealed, and more than 80 percent of appealed denials overturned. AMA 2025 report: 94 percent of physicians report PA harms clinical outcomes and nearly one-third witnessed a serious adverse event from PA delays. LULAC cites nearly one-third of Latinos enrolled in Medicaid, Hispanic Americans as approximately 31 percent of Medicaid enrollees, and higher disease and affordability burdens among Latino Medicare beneficiaries.
- **Studies or research referenced:** KFF Medicare Advantage PA report; AMA prior authorization report; Medicaid and Latino enrollment analyses; HHS report on Latino Medicare enrollees; 2024 study on racial and ethnic disparities in PA for cancer patients; KFF LEP report; MedCOD translation study; CRS language-access report; National Health Law Program Title VI and Section 1557 explainer; additional works cited list.
- **Examples provided:** High denial rates and high appeal-overturn rates as triggers for oversight; Latino beneficiaries, limited-English-proficient patients, and protected populations as groups requiring disparity monitoring; denial notices and appeal instructions as communications needing language access.

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** Latino beneficiaries, Medicaid and Medicare enrollees, patients with limited English proficiency, patients subject to PA and step therapy, physicians, providers, health plans, PBMs, regulators, and protected populations experiencing disparities.
- **Economic implications:** LULAC discusses medication affordability and patient costs but does not provide quantified cost estimates for implementation. It suggests accountability could reduce wasteful denials, appeals, and delayed care.
- **Technical feasibility:** LULAC supports FHIR-based APIs and standardized workflows but argues technical modernization must be accompanied by policy accountability and multilingual access.
- **Patient care impact:** The comment argues that PA reform should reduce inappropriate denials, prevent delayed care, improve access to physician-prescribed treatment, and address disparities in outcomes and access.

## 10. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

- **Overall position:** Mixed / Concerned
- **Tone:** Critical, equity-focused, policy-oriented
- **Priority level:** High

## 11. KEY QUOTES

1. "Visibility, however, is not reform." - Context: Core argument for accountability.
2. "Technology should improve care" - Context: Concern about accelerating denials.
3. "Language access is a legal obligation" - Context: Request for multilingual communications.
4. "Accountability is." - Context: Conclusion that transparency is not the end goal.

## 12. THEMES

- [x] **PROVIDER-BURDEN** - LULAC cites physician administrative burden and time spent navigating utilization management.
- [x] **HEALTH-EQUITY** - The comment centers Latino beneficiaries, Medicaid reliance, limited English proficiency, and disparate denial impacts.
- [x] **PATIENT-ACCESS** - LULAC frames the rule's success around whether patients receive medically necessary and physician-prescribed care.
- [x] **TRANSPARENCY** - The comment supports reporting but insists transparency must trigger oversight and enforcement.
- [x] **TECHNICAL-FEASIBILITY** - LULAC supports FHIR APIs and standardized workflows but emphasizes that technology alone is insufficient.
- [x] **REGULATORY-AUTHORITY** - The comment asks CMS to use enforcement authority and corrective-action mechanisms when data reveal failure.
- [x] **EXISTING-WORKFLOWS** - It addresses step therapy, utilization management, appeal workflows, and denial-notice processes.
- [x] **STAKEHOLDER-COORDINATION** - The comment discusses regulators, plans, providers, PBMs, and patients as participants in a PA accountability framework.
